newsitem.title: UK: UK inflation goal threatened as recovery quickens.
newsitem.headline: UK inflation goal threatened as recovery quickens.

text.p: The British government looks set to miss its key 2.5 percent inflation target and may have to raise interest rates ahead of the next election, due by May, as economic growth gathers pace, a growing number of analysts say.

Economic recovery, entering its fifth year, is clearly speeding up and strong consumer demand could drive prices higher. Lower commodity costs and subdued factory gate prices may not now be enough to keep a lid on inflation.
"We've never thought inflation would hit its target and we're more convinced than ever after the latest data," said Geoffrey Dicks, UK economist at NatWest Markets.

Latest retail prices data showed the RPIX index, which excludes volatile mortgage interest payments, rose 2.9 percent in September, some way above the 2.5 percent target which the government had hoped to meet by the end of this parliament.

That is prompting the National Institute of Economic and Social Research, among others, to revise upwards its inflation forecasts for next year. "In the Bank of England's language, we don't see a greater than evens chance of the government hitting its target," said economist Garry Young.
Other data suggests pay settlements may head higher, too. There was a sharp 35,600 fall in unemployment in September, taking the jobless total to a five-and-a-half year low.
Skills shortages in the labour market will soon put more upward pressure on earnings, which are already growing.

Economists gloomy on inflation said too much faith had been placed in lower commodity costs and output prices when the components that have the most immediate impact on retail prices have headed higher.
"There are already signs that the impact of producer prices has not been disinflationary. Higher oil and food prices have made themselves felt in retail prices," said Dicks.
Factory gate prices reversed their recent trend and headed higher in September, up 0.4 percent on the month for a 2.2 percent year-on-year rate, bad news for the inflation optimists.
"It's touch and go whether the government hits the target. The rising oil price has certainly knocked inflation off track," said Neil Blake, research director at Business Strategies Ltd.

But greater risks still lie in the strength of demand which might be the trigger for higher rates. Bank of England Governor Eddie George has already said he is concerned at its strength and wants to see base rates back up at 6.0 percent from 5.75.

So far, Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke has ignored his advice while admitting consumer spending will probably accelerate. Tax cuts and windfall gains from building society mergers and flotations have yet to fully hit home and promise to stimulate demand further.
There is also a danger that retailers, which were hit badly during the downturn, may take the opportunity to rebuild their battered margins as demand accelerates.
A huge 5.2 percent rise in clothing and footwear prices in September may have partly reflected margin rebuilding.

But Blake said shops will be able to make some progress due to lower costs. "That rise might have been a one off, given the unclear timing of when summer sales end. Retailers are eager to rebuild their margins but lower costs can help them do that to an extent."

The Bank of England has to date been reasonably relaxed about margin-building, making an assumption that the decline in retailers' margins suffered in the downturn will not be fully reversed as activity picks up. It believes competition will keep margins, and prices, low.
But sources close to the central bank said it is getting slightly more concerned and may well point out this risk in its next inflation report, due next month.
There are some tricks the Chancellor could pull in the budget if he is really determined to hit the inflation target.

"If he didn't index value added taxes in the budget, that would help," said Blake. "But given the state of the public finances, he can't really afford to do it. He'll save his fire for income tax cuts."
And sterling's recent rally may come to Clarke's aid. It has appreciated 5.8 percent on a trade-weighted basis since early August, definitely a sort of monetary tightening.
But economists said even if Clarke did bite the bullet and raise rates, it would be too late to drive prices down before May. "All Clarke can really do is hope and pray," said Dicks.
